newsitem.title: GERMANY: German industrial fire rates to fall again -broker.
newsitem.headline: German industrial fire rates to fall again -broker.

text.p: German insurance broker Jaspers Industrie Assekuranz (JIA) said it expects a further drop in German industrial fire rates for 1997.

"We see a decline of between five and 15 percent," Stephan Zilkens, one of JIA's managing directors, said on Wednesday. "But this will be far more modest than the 1996 renewals, when for some clients we could achieve a halving of rates."
From 1998 onwards, Zilkens expects "dramatically increasing prices" in industrial insurance again.

In addition, the market would probably split in two. Some industrial companies, notably the larger ones, would increase risk protection, increase their deductibles and find more intelligent insurance solutions. Insurance companies would seek "dramatic increases" from the others, Zilkens said.

Klaus Nowitzky, another JIA managing director, said that the broker's turnover stagnated in 1996 due to the soft market at a premium level of around 750 million marks. Commission turnover remained at 90 million marks.

Nowitzky refused to give a profit figure, but said that the company was operating in the black. However, 1996 profits would be down 25 percent. JIA has 400 staff in nine offices and some 2,500 clients, mostly medium- sized industrial enterprises.

The company is owned by Deutsche Bank with 20 percent, international broker Alexander & Alexander with another 20 percent and three families, holding the remaining 60 percent. Nowitzky said he does not expect any major changes to the ownership structure.
Some 15 percent of the business involves the international A&A network. JIA owns 50 percent of specialist broker Versicherungsstelle Zellstoff und Papier (VZP), which caters for the paper industry.

The remaining 50 percent is held by 177 companies from that industry. VZP's premium volume in 1996 was an unchanged 130 million marks, said Nowitzky, with commission income amounting to 15 million marks. In paper making, VZP had a market share of 60 percent and in paper processing some 25 percent. "The loss development is very favourable, we have loss ratios below 50 percent," he said.
